### The desk with one drawer

Picture a brilliant consultant who works in a room with a single small desk.

Whatever you want them to consider, you must place on that desk before they start. Your
instructions. The customer's message. The three policy pages they will need. The notes from
earlier in the conversation. The list of things they are allowed to do.

The desk is not large. When it is full, something has to come off — and here is the part that
decides whether your system works: **they will not tell you what fell off.** They will answer
confidently using whatever is still in front of them.

Everything you put on that desk is called the **context**, and the size of the desk is the
**context window** — measured in tiles (Week 25). Deciding what goes on it, in what order, on
every single request, is a bigger job than writing a good instruction. It has a name now, and in
2026 it is what "prompt engineer" jobs turned into: **context engineering**.

### What is actually on the desk

Six things, and most systems have all six:

1. **The system prompt** — role, rules, format (Module 1).
2. **Examples** — the few-shot cases from Module 2, if you kept them.
3. **Tool definitions** — the list of functions the model may ask for (Week 30). These cost tiles
   too, and people forget: twenty tools with long descriptions can be a third of your window.
4. **Retrieved passages** — whatever Week 27's search returned for this question.
5. **Conversation history** — everything said so far, re-sent every turn.
6. **The user's actual message** — often the smallest thing on the desk.

Add those up on a busy request and the arithmetic is sobering. Which leads to the first real skill.

### Budget the window like money

Do not wait to discover the limit — assign it. A workable starting split for a 100,000-tile
window, which you then tune with measurements:

| What | Budget | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System prompt + rules | 800 | Fixed, cacheable, small |
| Tool definitions | 1,500 | Grows quietly as tools are added |
| Few-shot examples | 1,000 | Drop first if retrieval is strong |
| Retrieved passages | 6,000 | The tunable one — see below |
| Conversation history | 4,000 | Summarise beyond this |
| The answer | 2,000 | Reserved, or generation is truncated |
| **Headroom** | **the rest** | Never plan to fill the window |

Two rules that come out of writing this table honestly. **Reserve room for the answer** — a
window that is full of input has no room to reply, and the failure looks like a truncated
sentence. And **never plan to use all of it**: the model's use of material degrades before the
hard limit, so a full window is a slow window and a worse answer.

### More context is not better context

The instinct is to send everything — the whole document, all twenty passages, the entire history —
because surely more information can only help.

It does not, for two reasons you can verify yourself.

**Relevant material gets diluted.** Send the one right paragraph plus nineteen mediocre ones and
the right one now competes for attention with nineteen distractions. Retrieval quality (Week 28)
matters more than retrieval quantity, and sending your top 5 usually beats sending your top 20.

**Position affects use.** Material at the very beginning and very end of a long context is used
more reliably than material buried in the middle — a well-documented tendency worth designing
around. So the single most important passage should not be sixth of twelve.

### The order that serves two masters at once

Happily, the ordering that helps the model is the same one that saves you money.

Put the **most stable content first** — system prompt, rules, tool definitions, examples — then
retrieved passages, then history, and the **user's message and task instruction last**.

- For the model: the instruction is the final thing read, and is followed most reliably.
- For the bill: providers cache the *prefix* of a prompt, so an unchanged beginning can be re-used
  at a fraction of the cost. Put anything volatile early — a timestamp, a session id, a greeting
  with the user's name — and you break the cache for everything after it, silently, on every
  request.

That single mistake is one of the most expensive in this course, and nothing about it looks
broken.

### What to do when it will not fit

Four moves, in the order you should try them:

1. **Retrieve less, better.** Five good passages beat twenty mediocre ones. This is usually the
   whole fix.
2. **Trim what you re-send.** Tool outputs especially: return the first rows and a count, never a
   whole table.
3. **Summarise the old.** Keep the last few turns verbatim; replace older ones with a running
   summary (Week 30 M3).
4. **Store it outside and fetch on demand.** Anything durable belongs in the library, not the
   window — which is Week 27 pointed inward.

<Check>
**The answer to the opening question, plainly.** The desk is finite, so context engineering is
**deciding what earns its place on it, in what order, on every call** — the system prompt,
examples, tool definitions, retrieved passages, history and the user's message all compete for the
same window. More is not better: extra material dilutes the passage that mattered, and things in
the middle of a long context are used less reliably than things at either end. So you budget the
window like money, reserve room for the answer, put stable content first and the instruction last
— which is simultaneously what the model reads best and what the cache pays you for.
</Check>

<Accordion title="Checkpoint — 6 questions before you continue">
1. **What is the context window?** The finite space holding everything the model sees on one call, measured in tiles.
2. **Name the six things competing for it.** System prompt, examples, tool definitions, retrieved passages, conversation history, the user's message.
3. **Why is sending more context often worse?** The relevant material is diluted by distractions, and middle-of-context material is used less reliably.
4. **Why reserve budget for the answer?** Input that fills the window leaves no room to generate; the reply is truncated.
5. **What order should a prompt be in, and why does it help twice?** Stable content first, instruction last — best adherence, and it preserves the cacheable prefix.
6. **What are the four moves when context will not fit?** Retrieve less but better, trim what you re-send, summarise older turns, and store the rest outside for retrieval.
</Accordion>

### The question this page leaves open

You now decide what the model sees, and in what order. Which makes that decision **production
logic** — as consequential as any code path, and currently written in English in a file somebody
edited last month without telling anyone.

Treating it the way you treat code — versioned, reviewed, tested, revertible — is
[Module 5 — Prompts are code](/curriculum/p4/week-29/5-prompts-are-code).

  <Tab title="🔵 Layer 2 — Build">
    **You ship code for a living?** This layer is yours — trade-offs, real tools, real versions.

    The endpoint worked for six months, then a customer with 400 conversation turns and eleven
    attached documents hit it and everything after their fourth question was answered from
    nothing. This layer is the assembly code that prevents that.

### Assemble the context explicitly

Do not build prompts by string concatenation scattered through your codebase. Build them in one
place, with a budget, and make the truncation decisions visible:

```python
# context.py — one place that decides what the model sees
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Budget:
    system: int = 800
    tools: int = 1_500
    examples: int = 1_000
    retrieved: int = 6_000
    history: int = 4_000
    reserved_for_answer: int = 2_000

@dataclass
class Assembled:
    system: str
    messages: list
    dropped: dict = field(default_factory=dict)      # what did not fit, and why

def assemble(system, tools, examples, passages, history, question, b=Budget(), count=len):
    dropped = {}
    # 1. retrieved: keep highest-scoring passages until the budget is spent
    kept, used = [], 0
    for p in sorted(passages, key=lambda p: -p.score):
        if used + count(p.text) > b.retrieved:
            dropped.setdefault("passages", 0); dropped["passages"] += 1
            continue
        kept.append(p); used += count(p.text)
    # 2. history: newest turns verbatim, older ones summarised
    hist, used_h = [], 0
    for turn in reversed(history):
        if used_h + count(turn.text) > b.history:
            dropped["history_turns"] = dropped.get("history_turns", 0) + 1
            continue
        hist.insert(0, turn); used_h += count(turn.text)
    # 3. stable first, volatile last — for adherence and for the cache
    return Assembled(system=system,
                     messages=[*examples, *[p.as_message() for p in kept], *hist,
                               {"role": "user", "content": question}],
                     dropped=dropped)
```

The `dropped` field is the point. **Silent truncation is the enemy**; a system that records what
it left out can be debugged, alerted on, and explained to a customer.

### Trade-offs

**Summarise vs. drop.** Summarising old turns preserves the thread and costs a model call;
dropping is free and loses the thread. Summarise when the conversation has state ("as I said, my
order is TX-4471"); drop when each question is independent.

**More passages vs. better passages.** Every extra passage costs tiles and dilutes attention. If
adding passages 6–20 does not move your eval score, they are pure cost — measure it rather than
assuming.

**Long window vs. retrieval.** A very large window tempts you to skip retrieval and paste
everything. It is usually slower, dearer and *less* accurate than retrieving well — the window
size changed what is possible, not what is wise.

### Instrument it

Log per request: tiles by section (system / tools / examples / retrieved / history), what was
dropped, and the answer's tile count. Two dashboards fall out for free — a cost breakdown you can
act on (Week 34 M3), and an early warning when history growth is about to start evicting
instructions.

  <Tab title="🟣 Layer 3 — Edge">
    **For anyone who has shipped this and been burned.** Internals, scale, numbers.

### The window is not uniform

Treat the context window as a space with *positions*, not a bucket. Material at the start and end
is used more reliably than material in the middle, and the effect grows with length. Design
consequences:

- Rank retrieved passages by score and place the strongest **last**, immediately before the
  question, rather than first.
- Never bury the task instruction in the middle of a long context.
- When evaluating retrieval, measure whether the answer used the passage you provided —
  groundedness (Week 33 M3) — not merely whether the passage was present.

### Cache economics, and the ordering they force

Prefix caching turns prompt order into a cost decision. The rule is mechanical: **everything before
the first volatile byte is cacheable; everything after it is not.** Which means:

- A per-user greeting at the top of a shared system prompt destroys the cache for every request.
- Injecting `"Today is {date}"` at the start costs more than injecting it just before the question.
- Stable tool definitions belong high; a session id belongs low.

The failure is invisible: correct answers, unremarkable latency, and a bill several times larger
than necessary. It shows up in Week 34's cost breakdown as an unexpectedly low cache-hit rate.

### What breaks at very long context

Three things, all worth measuring on your own workload before relying on a large window:

1. **Attention cost.** Cost and latency grow faster than linearly with length (Week 25 M3), so a
   200k-tile prompt is not twice a 100k one.
2. **Retrieval-in-context degrades.** The ability to *use* a fact in the window declines with
   distance and distraction long before the hard limit.
3. **KV cache memory.** On self-hosted serving (Week 26 M5), per-conversation memory scales with
   context length, so long contexts reduce how many users one card can serve.

The practical rule that follows: **a bigger window is a safety margin, not a design.** Systems that
treat it as a design get slower and dearer without getting better.

### Papers and primary sources

- [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) — Liu et al., 2023. Read this for the position effect and how it was measured.
- [Anthropic — prompt caching](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching). Read this for what is cacheable and the exact ordering rules.
- [Anthropic — context editing and compaction](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/context-editing). Read this for provider-side strategies for long conversations.

### Stretch challenge

Instrument your endpoint to record tiles by section for a week of real traffic, then plot the
distribution. Find the p99 request. Most teams discover one section they never thought about —
usually tool definitions or history — consuming a third of the window, and can halve their p99
context without touching answer quality.

## Hands-on

Instrument one endpoint of your own to report tiles by section and what was dropped. Run it on
twenty real requests. The section you did not expect to be large is where your next improvement
is.

## Apply it at work

**For the student.** "I budgeted the context window and logged evictions" is a sentence almost no
junior candidate can say, and it demonstrates systems thinking rather than API familiarity.

**For the professional.** Check your prompt for a volatile value near the top. Moving it down is a
ten-minute change that can materially cut a monthly bill.

## Assessment

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="6 concept questions">
  1. What competes for the context window? (System prompt, examples, tool definitions, retrieved passages, history, user message — plus reserved room for the answer.)
  2. Why can adding passages lower answer quality? (Dilution: the relevant passage competes with distractions, and middle positions are used less reliably.)
  3. Where should the strongest retrieved passage go, and why? (Last, next to the question — position affects use.)
  4. What single mistake silently destroys prefix caching? (Volatile content — a timestamp, session id or personalised greeting — placed early in the prompt.)
  5. Why is a bigger window a margin rather than a design? (Cost and latency grow faster than linearly, use degrades with distance, and KV memory limits concurrency.)
  6. What must a context assembler always report? (What it dropped, and why — silent truncation is undebuggable.)
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Coding challenge">
  Implement `assemble()` with per-section budgets, score-ordered passage selection, newest-first
  history retention, reserved answer space, and a `dropped` report. Hidden tests check: the total
  never exceeds the window minus the answer reservation; the highest-scoring passage is always
  kept; dropped counts are accurate; and stable sections always precede volatile ones.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Interview questions (junior / mid / senior)">
  - **Junior:** "What is a context window, and what is in it besides the user's question?"
  - **Mid:** "Long conversations start giving worse answers after about twenty turns. What is happening and how would you fix it?"
  - **Senior:** "Design the context strategy for an assistant with a 200k window, RAG over 2M documents, 30-tool catalogue and multi-day conversations. Include budgets, eviction policy, ordering, and how you would prove the design is right."
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Common mistakes

- **Filling the window because it is there.** More context dilutes; measure before adding.
- **No reservation for the answer.** The reply gets truncated and it looks like a model failure.
- **Volatile content at the top.** Silently destroys prefix caching, multiplying cost.
- **Burying the best passage in the middle.** Position matters; put it last.
- **Truncating silently.** Always record what was dropped, or the failure is undebuggable.
